subject: Binary and bits — how computers store everything as 0s and 1s
title: Why Do Computers Use 1s and 0s? Binary and Transistors Explained.
angle: from the hardware up: transistors as tiny switches
why: Shows why a computer only knows on and off, and how those switches add up to numbers and text. 5M views, 143K likes.

subject: Big O notation — how to judge if code stays fast as data grows
title: Big-O Notation in 100 Seconds
angle: the whole idea in 100 seconds, shown on small code examples
why: You get the common speeds (constant, linear, quadratic, log) and how to spot each one in a loop, fast enough to watch twice.

subject: Hashing — turning any data into a short fingerprint
title: Hashing Algorithms and Security - Computerphile
angle: Tom Scott shows hashing through real uses: checking a download, storing passwords
why: You see what a hash is for, why a tiny change flips the whole fingerprint, and why old hashes like MD5 get broken and replaced. 1.66M views, 36K likes.

subject: Data structures — lists, maps, trees: picking the right box for data
title: 10 Key Data Structures We Use Every Day
angle: each structure shown inside a real product you already use
why: Animated diagrams of lists, maps, trees, graphs and more, each tied to where it really lives: your browser history, a spreadsheet, a map app, a database. 455K views, 16K likes.

subject: Recursion — a function that solves a problem by calling itself
title: What on Earth is Recursion? - Computerphile
angle: factorial worked by hand, call by call, then compared with a plain loop
why: You watch each call wait for the next one and then unwind back up, which is the part that makes recursion click. 781K views, 26K likes.

subject: How the internet works — packets, IP addresses, DNS
title: What happens when you type a URL into your browser?
angle: follows one real action, typing a URL, from keypress to page
why: No theory first: you follow one request as DNS finds the server's address, a connection opens, and the page comes back. Each step is something your apps do on every API call. 485K views, 19K likes.

subject: Caching — keeping a copy close by to avoid slow work
title: Memory, Cache Locality, and why Arrays are Fast (Data Structures and Optimization)
angle: one cache taken apart, the CPU's, proven with code and real timings
why: You see why reading memory in order is fast and jumping around is slow, with benchmarks on screen. It shows what a cache actually does, not just where caches live. 343K views, 11.6K likes.

subject: Concurrency — doing many things at once without breaking data
title: Atomic Operations - Computerphile
angle: Matt Godbolt builds a fair lock from one atomic step, like a deli counter's ticket machine
why: You will see how threads can wait their turn fairly, like taking a number at a deli counter: everyone gets a place in line, so nobody waits forever. It is built on an atomic operation, a step that can never be cut in half.

subject: How neural networks learn — weights, errors, gradient descent
title: AI Doesn't Know Anything. It Just Passes Tests.
angle: the very basics, no math: a story of bots that get tested and tweaked
why: No formulas and no code. Cartoon bots try a task, get graded, and the best ones get small changes, over and over, until they get good. You leave knowing the big idea: nobody writes the rules, the machine is shaped by tests. 12.6M views, 667K likes.

subject: Tokens and embeddings — how language models turn words into numbers
title: Large Language Models explained briefly
angle: the big picture first, with animations, no formulas
why: You see how a chatbot works at heart: it guesses the next word, again and again. Along the way you see words being turned into lists of numbers, so the computer can work with them. Made for a general audience. 8.6M views, 205K likes.

subject: Binary and bits — how computers store everything as 0s and 1s
title: How to count to 1000 on two hands
angle: targets the weak spot: place values, counted on your own fingers (1, 2, 4, 8...)
why: Each finger is worth double the one before, so you feel how binary place values work instead of memorising them. Try it along with the video: by the end, reading a binary number becomes simple addition. 457K views, 13K likes.
